title: Biochemistry I: Proteins, Enzymes & Metabolism
description: A mechanistic and quantitative introduction to protein structure, enzyme kinetics, thermodynamics, and central metabolism, with an animal-cell focus and an explicit photosynthesis boundary.

modifications: Linked the first four lesson pairs to outcomes 1–4. Reassociated the preserved ligand-occupancy and pool-versus-flux questions with their binding and flux objectives, and added direct practice for protein structure levels and regulatory layers. Existing numeric prompts and keys remain unchanged. The course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

prerequisites.statement: General Chemistry II; Organic Chemistry I recommended

outcomes.description: Interpret protein sequence, structure, and binding models.
Track carbon, electrons, and energy through central metabolism.
Explain pathway control through multiple regulatory layers.
Evaluate protein separation and purification data to judge selectivity, recovery and enrichment.

lesson_objectives.description: Describe primary through quaternary structure.
Distinguish binding affinity, specificity, and cooperativity.
Distinguish competitive and noncompetitive model signatures.
Use catalytic efficiency and model assumptions carefully.
Track oxidation state and carbon fate through glycolysis and respiration.
Relate redox carriers and proton motive force to ATP synthesis.
Calculate net ATP-pool change from stipulated synthesis and utilization rates and distinguish a stable pool from ongoing ATP turnover.
Identify control at substrate supply, allostery, covalent modification, and expression.
Predict how perturbing one pathway affects connected fluxes.
Compute initial rates, turnover number and catalytic efficiency from Michaelis–Menten parameters.
Predict apparent Km and Vmax for competitive and pure noncompetitive inhibition and use them to diagnose an inhibitor's mode.
Evaluate how linearized plots and assay conditions can distort parameter estimates.
Calculate the actual free-energy change of a reaction from its standard value and the concentrations of reactants and products.
Compute the standard free-energy change and equilibrium constant of a reaction coupled to ATP hydrolysis.
Convert a difference in reduction potential into a free-energy change and interpret where energy is released in electron transport.
Use the dissociation constant to compute fractional occupancy at a given free ligand concentration and interpret K_d.
Account for ligand depletion with the exact quadratic solution and judge when the simple hyperbolic equation is adequate.
Use the Hill equation to describe cooperative binding and compare oxygen unloading by cooperative and non-cooperative carriers.
Compute the protonation state and the net charge of an amino acid or a short chain at a given pH from its pKa values.
Calculate the isoelectric point of amino acids with and without an ionizable side chain.
Predict how a protein's net charge changes with pH and what that implies for solubility, migration and binding to an ion-exchange resin.
Convert between the free energy of unfolding, the equilibrium constant and the fraction of protein that is folded for a two-state protein.
Use the linear dependence of unfolding free energy on denaturant concentration to find a stability in water and a denaturation midpoint.
Evaluate how a mutation, temperature or aggregation changes stability, and explain why marginal stability matters for proteostasis.
Compute AMP from the adenylate kinase equilibrium and the adenylate energy charge, and show how a small fall in ATP amplifies AMP.
Balance carbon, ATP and NADH through glycolysis and lactate fermentation and compute the glucose uptake needed to meet an ATP demand.
Explain allosteric control of phosphofructokinase and distinguish a change in a metabolite pool from a change in flux.
Calculate the proton-motive force from its electrical and pH components and the free energy per mole of protons.
Estimate the minimum and actual protons per ATP and the ATP yield per NADH, FADH₂ and glucose.
Predict how proton leak or an uncoupler changes ATP made per oxygen and the whole-body ATP turnover implied by oxygen uptake.
Distinguish a change in a pool size from a change in flux using a steady-state model of a two-step pathway.
Use flux control coefficients and their summation to predict how a change in one enzyme alters pathway flux.
Match the layers of regulation of an enzyme to their time scales and compute the time for a change in enzyme amount to take effect.
Summarize replicate initial rates by condition and substrate concentration.
Estimate Vmax and Km from a double-reciprocal fit and the apparent Km under an inhibitor, and compute the inhibition constant.
Evaluate the mode of inhibition, the limits of linearized fits and the assay conditions that make initial rates trustworthy.
Compute the glucose uptake and lactate output a cell needs to maintain ATP when oxidative phosphorylation is blocked.
Interpret changes in the lactate/pyruvate ratio and in tracer labeling as signals of redox state and carbon source.
Design a measurement that separates impaired oxidative phosphorylation from a primary glycolytic defect, and state what each result would show.
Choose a protein-separation method from evidence about charge relative to pI, molecular size or a selective binding interaction, and state its limits.
Calculate total protein, total activity, specific activity, recovery and fold enrichment from fraction data, and distinguish enrichment from a claim of homogeneity.
Account for carbon and cofactor outputs from one acetyl-CoA turn of the citric acid cycle and distinguish those outputs from pyruvate oxidation and electron transport.
Explain how withdrawal and replenishment of cycle intermediates and changing redox or energy demand can affect pathway flux.
Interpret mass-isotopologue evidence and distinguish changes in labeling from claims about pathway flux.
Explain the three gluconeogenic bypasses and calculate the ATP, GTP and NADH input needed to form glucose from pyruvate.
Interpret reciprocal regulation of glycolysis and gluconeogenesis and identify carbon sources that can or cannot support net glucose synthesis.
Trace glucose into glycogen and glycogen residues into glucose 6-phosphate, including nucleotide cost and the roles of phosphorylase and the debranching enzyme.
Predict reciprocal glycogen synthesis and breakdown responses and distinguish the systemic role of liver glycogen from the local role of muscle glycogen.
Calculate oxidative-branch NADPH and carbon dioxide outputs from glucose 6-phosphate and distinguish NADPH production from ATP yield.
Explain how reversible nonoxidative reactions connect pentose needs to glycolytic carbon and how NADP availability relates to oxidative-branch flux.
Calculate beta-oxidation cycle count, acetyl-CoA and reducing-equivalent outputs for an even-chain saturated fatty acyl-CoA, and account for activation cost when starting from a free fatty acid.
Integrate beta-oxidation with the citric acid cycle and electron transport using stated P/O assumptions, and explain carnitine transport and its regulation.
Trace the two nitrogen atoms and the carbon atom of urea to their immediate donors, and calculate ATP molecules and high-energy phosphate equivalents consumed.
Relate transamination, glutamate, aspartate, urea-cycle compartmentation, CPS1 regulation and fumarate return to central metabolism.
Match representative amino-acid carbon skeletons to pyruvate, acetyl-CoA/acetoacetate or citric-acid-cycle entry points and classify their carbon as glucogenic, ketogenic or both.
Explain how transamination separates amino nitrogen from carbon fate and why acetyl-CoA alone cannot support net glucose synthesis in mammals.
Identify the three ketone bodies and explain how acetyl-CoA, mitochondrial redox and gluconeogenic demand relate to hepatic ketogenesis.
Trace ketone-body use in extrahepatic mitochondria and explain why liver exports rather than oxidizes the ketones it makes.
Distinguish canonical SCOT-dependent oxidative ketolysis from reported SCOT-independent anabolic use in hepatocytes, and state the evidence’s species and pathway boundary.
Calculate conditional ATP-equivalent output from acetoacetate and D-beta-hydroxybutyrate under stated P/O and SCOT opportunity-cost assumptions.
Calculate the cytosolic acetyl-CoA, malonyl-CoA, ATP and NADPH requirements for palmitate synthesis while stating the accounting boundary.
Explain citrate-shuttle acetyl-CoA supply, acetyl-CoA carboxylase control and malonyl-CoA inhibition of mitochondrial fatty-acid entry.
Trace cholesterol biosynthesis from acetyl-CoA through mevalonate and explain sterol feedback on HMG-CoA reductase and LDL-receptor expression.
Trace dietary and endogenous lipoprotein routes and distinguish the functions of key apolipoproteins, lipoprotein lipase and LDL receptor.
Trace the de novo purine and pyrimidine pathways to IMP and UMP, distinguish their construction order and explain nucleotide-branch control.
Explain purine salvage, ribonucleotide reduction and thymidylate formation as linked routes that support nucleotide pools and DNA precursors.
Calculate PRPP use across synthetic de novo purine synthesis and purine salvage, then separately account for ATP and GTP used at the IMP branch point.
Trace glycerol-3-phosphate acylation through phosphatidic acid and diacylglycerol to triacylglycerol, and connect storage to hepatic VLDL export.
Compare intracellular adipose lipolysis with capillary lipoprotein lipase and trace fatty-acid and glycerol products into downstream metabolism.
Calculate total protein and activity, specific activity, activity recovery and fold enrichment from synthetic fraction data.
Select an orthogonal separation property and interpret why enrichment and activity do not establish homogeneity.
Interpret isotope-tracing evidence for amino-acid carbon fate in a stated model, distinguishing substrate contribution to biosynthesis from net glucose production and whole-body inference.
Calculate a labeled-ribose fraction from a synthetic isotopomer distribution and explain why labeling alone does not quantify pathway flux.
Convert a stated nitrogen-disposal load into a stoichiometric urea amount and the associated ATP-equivalent demand under an explicit closed-balance assumption.
Calculate a synthetic hepatocyte cholesterol-pool balance from input and output rates and distinguish that cellular pool from circulating LDL concentration.

duration.equivalent_structure: Proposed 14-week undergraduate sequence, not measured semester equivalence. It stages protein recognition before quantitative binding, thermodynamics before metabolic applications, and network perturbation before quantitative flux control. The schedule includes ungraded synthetic-data practice, two virtual data-analysis labs, eight open homework practice sets, midterm and cumulative final review practice and an optional protein-state project with Case studio self-checks; there are no approved summative assessments or physical laboratory sequence.

weeks.title: Amino-acid charge, nitrogen disposal and carbon metabolism

workload.basis: Not measured. Legacy nominal credit and display-time labels are not retained as workload estimates.

modules.title: Protein structure and molecular recognition

lessons.title: Protein structure and molecular recognition
lessons.worked_example: For a simple 1:1 interaction at equilibrium with negligible ligand depletion, Kd equals the free ligand concentration at half occupancy. At 12 µM free ligand and Kd 4 µM, θ = 12/(4 + 12) = 0.75, or 75%; this is an equilibrium fraction, not a rate.

modules.title: Enzyme mechanisms and inhibition

lessons.title: Enzyme mechanisms and inhibition
lessons.worked_example: Without inhibitor, Vmax is 100 µmol/min and Km is 2 mM; at 2 mM substrate, rate is 50 µmol/min. A simple competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km to 8 mM while leaving Vmax unchanged, giving 20 µmol/min at the same substrate level. At saturating substrate, both ideal curves approach the same maximum rate.

modules.title: Bioenergetics and central carbon metabolism

lessons.title: Bioenergetics and central carbon metabolism
lessons.worked_example: Glycolysis yields 2 mol net ATP directly per mol glucose; five mol glucose yield 10 mol directly. A separate ATP amount balance with synthesis 146 µmol/min and use 134 µmol/min gives a pool increase of 12 µmol/min, not a concentration or pathway-flux estimate.

modules.title: Pathway regulation and metabolic integration

lessons.title: Pathway regulation and metabolic integration
lessons.worked_example: In a restricted two-input isotope-mixing model, fully labeled and unlabeled inputs that produce a 60% labeled product contribute in a 3:2 relative flux ratio. That result identifies neither absolute flux nor an unrestricted network solution; precursor labeling, turnover and exchange assumptions must be stated.

modules.title: Enzyme kinetics from data

lessons.title: Enzyme kinetics from data: estimating Vmax and Km, turnover, and diagnosing inhibition
lessons.worked_example: v(20 μM) = 100 × 20/25 = 80 μM/min; kcat = 166.7 s⁻¹; with α = 3, competitive Km,app = 15 μM gives 57.1 μM/min and noncompetitive Vmax,app = 33.3 μM/min gives 26.7 μM/min.

modules.title: Free energy, coupling and redox

lessons.title: Free energy in the cell: actual ΔG, coupled reactions and redox potential
lessons.worked_example: ATP hydrolysis at synthetic concentrations: ΔG = -30.5 + 2.577 ln(3.0×10⁻⁴) = -51.4 kJ/mol; hexokinase ΔG°′ = -16.7 kJ/mol; NADH to O₂: −2 × 96.485 × 1.135 = -219 kJ/mol.

modules.title: Binding equilibria and cooperativity

lessons.title: Binding equilibria: dissociation constants, ligand depletion and cooperative binding
lessons.worked_example: At K_d = 10 nM and 30 nM free ligand, θ = 0.75; with 50 nM receptor and ligand, the quadratic gives 32.1 nM complex rather than 41.7; a Hill carrier (n = 2.8, P₅₀ = 26) unloads 20.8% between 100 and 40 mmHg versus 3.8% for a hyperbolic one.

modules.title: Amino acids, charge and pH

lessons.title: Amino acids, charge and pH: titration, isoelectric points and the charge of a protein
lessons.worked_example: At pH 7.4 a lysine side chain is 99.9% protonated and a histidine side chain 3.8%; alanine has pI 6.015, glutamate 3.225, lysine 9.74 and histidine 7.585; a synthetic protein with 12 basic, 10 acidic and 4 histidine residues has net charge +1.9 at pH 7.4; a protein with pI 5.0 is net negative at pH 8.0 and binds an anion-exchange resin.

modules.title: Protein folding and stability

lessons.title: Protein folding and stability: two-state thermodynamics, denaturant m-values and marginal stability
lessons.worked_example: At 25 °C a ΔG_unfold of 10 kJ/mol gives K_u = 0.0177 and 0.983 folded; ΔG_H₂O = 25 kJ/mol with m = 10 kJ/mol per M gives a midpoint of 2.5 M and 5 kJ/mol at 2.0 M; a destabilization of 8 kJ/mol raises K_u 25-fold while the protein stays 99.9% folded.

modules.title: Glycolysis and its control

lessons.title: Glycolysis and its control: stoichiometry, energy charge and why AMP is a sensitive signal
lessons.worked_example: With ATP 3.0 mM and ADP 0.3 mM and K = 1, AMP is 0.03 mM and the energy charge 0.946; a 10% fall in ATP raises AMP 3.4-fold; meeting 6.0 mmol/(L·h) of ATP from glycolysis alone needs 3.0 mmol/(L·h) of glucose and releases 6.0 mmol/(L·h) of lactate; an activator that lowers K₀.₅ fourfold raises PFK-1 rate 5.7-fold.

modules.title: Mitochondrial bioenergetics

lessons.title: Mitochondrial bioenergetics: the proton-motive force, ATP yield and the cost of leak
lessons.worked_example: With Δψ = 150 mV and ΔpH = 0.75 the proton-motive force is 196 mV, or 18.9 kJ per mole of protons; making ATP needs at least 2.7 protons (about 4 in practice); complete oxidation of glucose gives 32 ATP, 5.3 per O₂; a 40% leak lowers this to 20.8 ATP per glucose; a resting oxygen uptake of 0.25 L/min implies about 60 mmol ATP/min.

modules.title: Flux control and regulation

lessons.title: Flux control and regulation: control coefficients, pool sizes and the layers of regulation
lessons.worked_example: In a two-step pathway doubling enzyme 1 raises both flux and the pool of A (4 mM/min, 8 mM), while halving enzyme 2 leaves flux at 2 mM/min and also doubles the pool (8 mM); with coefficients 0.5, 0.25 and 0.15 the fourth is 0.10; a 20% increase in enzyme 1 raises flux about 10%; an enzyme with a 2-day half-life reaches 90% of a new level in 6.6 days.

modules.title: Virtual laboratory: enzyme kinetics and inhibition

lessons.title: Virtual lab 1: enzyme kinetics and inhibition from replicate rates
lessons.worked_example: The control double-reciprocal fit gives Vmax 100.0 μM/min and Km 5.00 μM; with 4 μM inhibitor Vmax is unchanged and the apparent Km is 15.0 μM, so α = 3.00 and K_I = 2.00 μM for a competitive inhibitor; the double-reciprocal method is good for showing the pattern and poor for estimating parameters.

modules.title: Reading a metabolic perturbation

lessons.title: Reading a metabolic perturbation: ATP, lactate, redox and oxygen consumption
lessons.worked_example: With an ATP demand of 6.4 mmol/(L·h), 90% oxidative, glucose uptake is 0.50 mmol/(L·h); blocking oxidative phosphorylation raises it to 3.2 (6.4-fold) and lactate output 10-fold; lactate/pyruvate from 10 to 40 means a 4-fold more reduced cytosol; an M+3 lactate fraction of 0.48 with 50% labeled glucose means 96% came from medium glucose; oxygen consumption, the lactate/pyruvate ratio and an electron-acceptor rescue discriminate a chain block from a glycolytic defect.

modules.title: Protein purification and activity data

lessons.title: Protein purification as quantitative evidence: selectivity, recovery and specific activity
lessons.worked_example: A 12 mL synthetic fraction at 0.25 mg/mL contains 3.0 mg protein; at 90 U/mL it has 1,080 U activity, 18% recovery from 6,000 U and 360 U/mg, or sixfold enrichment over 60 U/mg starting activity.

lessons.title: Virtual purification lab: fraction recovery and enrichment
lessons.worked_example: The crude fraction contains 50 mL × 2.00 mg/mL = 100 mg total protein and 50 mL × 120 U/mL = 6,000 U total activity. Its specific activity is 60 U/mg and defines the baseline for recovery and enrichment. This comparison is meaningful only when the same assay definition is used for all fractions.

modules.title: The citric acid cycle: carbon, redox and replenishment

lessons.title: The citric acid cycle: carbon, reducing equivalents and replenishment
lessons.worked_example: Three mmol glucose supplies six acetyl-CoA and six TCA turns, producing 6.0 mmol GTP and 18 mmol NADH in the cycle. Pyruvate dehydrogenase adds 6 mmol NADH, for 24 mmol total in this boundary; glycolytic NADH is excluded. A synthetic [U-¹³C₆]glucose pulse raises the labeled citrate fraction from 30% to 60% (+30 percentage points), which demonstrates increased label incorporation but does not alone establish a doubled flux.

modules.title: Gluconeogenesis: bypass reactions and reciprocal control

lessons.title: Gluconeogenesis: bypass reactions, energy cost and reciprocal control
lessons.worked_example: Starting from pyruvate, 2.5 mol glucose requires 10 mol ATP, 5 mol GTP and 5 mol NADH. Per glucose, gluconeogenesis uses 4 ATP, 2 GTP and 2 NADH; six high-energy phosphate equivalents are split between ATP and GTP, and NADH is a separate reducing input. This accounting boundary excludes precursor formation.

modules.title: Glycogen storage, mobilization and tissue-specific control

lessons.title: Glycogen storage and mobilization: reciprocal control across tissues
lessons.worked_example: For an unbranched muscle-glycogen segment, 4 mol glucosyl residues release glucose 1-phosphate and then glucose 6-phosphate without a hexokinase investment. At 3 mol ATP net per residue to lactate, glycolysis yields 12 mol ATP. By contrast, storing 4 mol free glucose costs 8 mol ATP equivalents: one ATP for phosphorylation and one ATP equivalent per UDP-glucose activation.

modules.title: The pentose phosphate pathway: reducing power, ribose and carbon exchange

lessons.title: The pentose phosphate pathway: NADPH, ribose and carbon exchange
lessons.worked_example: For one oxidative-branch pass, each mole of glucose 6-phosphate produces 2 mol NADPH, 1 mol carbon dioxide and 1 mol ribulose 5-phosphate. Six moles therefore produce 12 mol NADPH, 6 mol carbon dioxide and 6 mol ribulose 5-phosphate, with no direct ATP product in this pathway boundary.

modules.title: Mitochondrial fatty-acid beta-oxidation and energy accounting

lessons.title: Fatty-acid beta-oxidation: acetyl-CoA and reducing equivalents
lessons.worked_example: Three mol palmitoyl-CoA (C16) yields 3 × (16/2 − 1) = 21 mol beta-oxidation turns and 3 × 8 = 24 mol acetyl-CoA. The starting boundary is activated palmitoyl-CoA, so free-fatty-acid activation cost is excluded.

modules.title: Amino-acid nitrogen handling and the urea cycle

lessons.title: Amino-acid nitrogen and the urea cycle
lessons.worked_example: Five mol of nitrogen atoms form 2.5 mol urea under the two-nitrogen-per-urea balance. At 3 ATP molecules and 4 high-energy phosphate equivalents per mol urea, this requires 7.5 mol ATP molecules and 10 mol high-energy phosphate equivalents.

modules.title: Amino-acid carbon skeletons and central-metabolism entry points

lessons.title: Amino-acid carbon skeletons: entry points and metabolic fate
lessons.worked_example: Alanine transfers its amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate and leaves a three-carbon pyruvate skeleton that can support gluconeogenesis; glutamate carries the nitrogen separately. In a distinct synthetic tracer example, the assigned BCAA contribution to lipogenic acetyl-CoA rises from 8.0% to 26.0% between cell states, a change of 18.0 percentage points that applies only to the stated model.

modules.title: Ketone-body synthesis and extrahepatic utilization

lessons.title: Ketone-body synthesis and use: a fasting fuel connection
lessons.worked_example: Two mmol D-BHB yield 43 mmol ATP-equivalents under an explicit model: P/O 2.5/1.5, one GTP per TCA turn, an extra NADH from D-BHB oxidation and one GTP-forming step bypassed by SCOT.

modules.title: Fatty-acid synthesis, triacylglycerol storage and reciprocal control

lessons.title: Fatty-acid synthesis and triacylglycerol storage and mobilization
lessons.worked_example: Twenty-four mol cytosolic acetyl-CoA provide three mol palmitate. The synthesis ledger forms 21 mol malonyl-CoA, consumes 21 mol ATP at acetyl-CoA carboxylase and 42 mol NADPH in fatty-acid synthase. The citrate-shuttle cost is outside this starting boundary. In a separate neutral-lipid ledger, 5 mol fully hydrolyzed triacylglycerol yields 15 mol fatty acids and 5 mol glycerol; this storage-mobilization count is independent of the cytosolic palmitate-synthesis boundary.

modules.title: Cholesterol synthesis and lipoprotein transport

lessons.title: Cholesterol synthesis and lipoprotein transport
lessons.worked_example: In a synthetic hepatocyte model, inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase lowers ER cholesterol. SREBP2 processing and expression of HMG-CoA reductase and the LDL receptor rise, but the inhibitor still suppresses enzyme activity. Increased LDL-receptor abundance can raise receptor-mediated LDL uptake, separating synthesis feedback from particle clearance.

modules.title: Purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis, salvage and DNA precursors

lessons.title: Nucleotide biosynthesis, salvage and deoxyribonucleotides
lessons.worked_example: Six mol IMP are split so that four mol form AMP and two mol form GMP. The AMP branch consumes four mol GTP; the GMP branch consumes two mol ATP. This counts only the branch conversions and excludes PRPP formation, construction of IMP, and later nucleotide phosphorylation. A separate mixed-route example uses 4 mol de novo IMP and 3 mol hypoxanthine salvage: 7 mol PRPP are consumed, while converting 2 mol IMP to AMP and 1 mol to GMP consumes 2 mol GTP and 1 mol ATP at those branch steps.

modules.title: Homework 1 practice: protein charge, nitrogen disposal and carbon fate

lessons.title: Homework 1 practice: protein charge, nitrogen disposal and carbon fate (open, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: A culture that routes 20.0 μmol nitrogen to urea and contains 2.5 million viable cells forms 20.0/2 = 10.0 μmol urea, spends 30.0 μmol ATP molecules or 40.0 μmol high-energy phosphate equivalents, and has 10.0/2.5 = 4.00 μmol urea per million cells. Normalize each culture this way before averaging the cultures in a condition.

modules.title: Homework 2 practice: stability, ligand depletion and replicate purification

lessons.title: Homework 2 practice: stability, ligand depletion and replicate purification (open, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: A run with a 30 mL crude extract at 3.0 mg/mL and 100 U/mL and a 4 mL final pool at 0.30 mg/mL and 450 U/mL has crude totals of 90 mg and 3,000 U and final totals of 1.2 mg and 1,800 U. Recovery is 60% and fold enrichment is 1,500/33.3 = 45; compute both within each run before averaging runs.

modules.title: Homework 3 practice: initial rates, efficiency and inhibition modes

lessons.title: Homework 3 practice: initial rates, efficiency and inhibition modes (open, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: An assay that forms 3.0 μM product in the first 5 minutes from 120 μM substrate has an early rate of 0.60 μM/min with 2.5% of the substrate used. A later window that gave a higher rate would signal a lag, activation or an assay artifact rather than an initial rate, so inspect the whole curve before choosing a window.

modules.title: Homework 4 practice: fitting replicate rates without a reciprocal plot

lessons.title: Homework 4 practice: fitting replicate rates without a reciprocal plot (open, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: For a fixed trial Km the best-fitting Vmax is Σ(v·x)/Σ(x²), with x = [S]/(Km + [S]) for each point. At Km = 4.0 μM the six control x values run from 0.200 to 0.889 and give Vmax ≈ 60.1 μM/min. Repeating this over nearby Km values and keeping the smallest residual sum of squares is a transparent check on a solver.

modules.title: Homework 5 practice: free energy, redox, labeling and nucleotide links

lessons.title: Homework 5 practice: free energy, redox, labeling and nucleotide links (open, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: For a step with ΔG°′ = −4.0 kJ/mol and a product/substrate ratio of 8.0 at 37 °C, ΔG = −4.0 + 2.577 × ln 8.0 = +1.36 kJ/mol, so the step runs backward because K′eq = 4.72 is below 8.0. A culture with 60% M+0 citrate has a 40% labeled fraction, a property of the pool at harvest rather than a rate.

modules.title: Homework 6 practice: energy charge, crossover and reciprocal control

lessons.title: Homework 6 practice: energy charge, crossover and reciprocal control (open, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: With ATP 2.0 mM, ADP 0.40 mM and an adenylate kinase constant of 1, AMP = 0.16/2.0 = 0.080 mM and the energy charge is (2.0 + 0.20)/(2.0 + 0.40 + 0.080) = 0.887. In a crossover, the step whose substrate ratio rises above 1 while its product ratio falls below 1 is the candidate control site.

modules.title: Homework 7 practice: fat and ketone fuels, proton leak and sterol feedback

lessons.title: Homework 7 practice: fat and ketone fuels, proton leak and sterol feedback (open, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: Lauroyl-CoA (C12:0) gives 5 turns and 6 acetyl-CoA, so 23 NADH, 11 FADH₂ and 6 GTP; from free laurate that is 23 × 2.5 + 11 × 1.5 + 6 − 2 = 78 ATP equivalents. A hepatocyte with synthesis 20, uptake 15, conversion 12 and export 8 μg/h gains 15 μg/h of cellular cholesterol, which is not a plasma LDL change.

modules.title: Homework 8 practice: control, NADPH supply and a respiratory block

lessons.title: Homework 8 practice: control, NADPH supply and a respiratory block (open, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: With an ATP demand of 8.0 mmol/(L·h) and 85% oxidative supply, glucose uptake is 0.85 × 8.0/32 + 0.15 × 8.0/2 = 0.8125 mmol/(L·h), lactate output 1.20 and oxygen use 1.275. If glycolysis alone must meet the demand, uptake becomes 4.0 and lactate 8.0, a 4.9-fold rise in glucose uptake.

modules.title: Protein-state project guide (optional, ungraded)

lessons.title: Protein-state project guide: charge, folding and ligand binding (optional, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: For rehearsal protein C at 2.5 M denaturant, ΔG_unfold = 22 − 8 × 2.5 = 2.0 kJ/mol, K_u = 0.4463 and f_folded = 0.6914, so R_F = 34.6 nM. The quadratic with L_T = 100 nM and K_d = 15 nM gives [RL] = 28.6 nM: 0.826 of the folded protein and 0.571 of the total protein, below the fictional 0.70 target.

modules.title: Week 7 midterm synthesis and review (ungraded)

lessons.title: Midterm synthesis: one enzyme preparation from charge to rate (weeks 1–7)
lessons.worked_example: Enzyme E in 1.5 M urea has ΔG_unfold = 20 − 10 × 1.5 = 5.0 kJ/mol, so K_u = 0.133 and 0.883 of it is folded: 17.7 of 20 nM is active. With kcat = 30 s⁻¹, Vmax = 31.8 μM/min rather than 36.0. A competitive inhibitor at 4.0 μM that raises Km from 6.0 to 14.0 μM gives α = 2.33 and K_I = 3.0 μM.

modules.title: Week 14 course synthesis and final review (ungraded)

lessons.title: Final synthesis: ledgers for energy, carbon, redox and control (weeks 8–14)
lessons.worked_example: A fasting hepatocyte model oxidizes 1.0 μmol palmitate to 8 acetyl-CoA (26 ATP equivalents after activation), oxidizes 2 acetyl-CoA in the cycle for 20 more and exports 3.0 μmol acetoacetate worth 57 ATP equivalents elsewhere. The total, 103, is three below complete oxidation in one place because SCOT bypasses one GTP-forming step per acetoacetate.

grading_policy.attempt_policy: Unlimited formative retries; no summative grade is awarded.
grading_policy.solution_release: Public practice solutions may be shown after an attempt. They are not production exam keys.
grading_policy.late_policy: No deadlines or late penalties exist in this partial package.
grading_policy.appeals: No instructor review workflow is implemented; report ambiguous practice items to repository maintainers.

accessibility.diagram_policy: The seed package contains no imported diagrams; newly authored diagrams require descriptions and individual license tracking.
known_issues: Unicode equations require structured mathematical alternatives and assistive-technology review.

history.summary: Preserved original compact prototype content in separate manifests and readings; labeled partial without semester or credit equivalency.

Added two original lessons (enzyme kinetics from data with inhibition fingerprints, and actual versus standard free energy, coupling and redox) with synthetic data, formative items with computed keys and retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Added an original lesson on binding equilibria (K_d, ligand depletion and cooperative Hill binding) with synthetic data, formative items with computed keys and retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Assessments with items now also list the course outcomes those items assess, derived from each item's lesson objective and that objective's outcome links. The rubric-only case lists none, and neither do the 4 prototype-unit assessments, whose objectives are not yet linked to an outcome. No readings, items or keys changed. The syllabus was regenerated from the manifest: it states the current version, lists every lesson with its item and card counts, and describes the current practice and limitations (it still described only the four original units). The course limitations shown to learners were also updated: they still described one formative check per lesson and the original numerical rules. The package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added a common-mistakes section to 2 original lessons that lacked one (biochemistry-5, biochemistry-6); each bullet names a mistake that the lesson's own text addresses. Fixed number formatting that an earlier authoring step left in learner-visible text: raw exponent notation (a number written with the letter e and a power of ten) and floating-point artifacts (a decimal with a long run of trailing digits) in item biochemistry-2:catalytic-efficiency. No answer key, tolerance or objective changed. The package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added a proposed 14-week schedule; six original lessons (amino acids, charge and the isoelectric point; protein folding and stability; glycolysis, energy charge and the AMP signal; mitochondrial bioenergetics and ATP yield; flux control and the layers of regulation; and reading a metabolic perturbation, which prepares the course case on a respiratory-chain inhibitor that lowers ATP and raises lactate); and a synthetic-data enzyme-kinetics lab with a competitive inhibitor. No new references were added. All activities remain ungraded practice; the package remains partial and unreviewed, gives no laboratory protocol or medical advice, and makes no claim about any compound or person.

Expanded the week-1 protein-structure reading with structural levels, interaction and folding context, ligand occupancy, affinity, specificity, cooperativity and binding-pathway distinctions. Existing questions, keys and objectives are unchanged. Three compact prototype readings remain in weeks 5, 9 and 12; the package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Expanded the week-5 enzyme reading with catalytic strategies, Michaelis-Menten assumptions, inhibition patterns, parameter interpretation and unit-aware catalytic efficiency. Existing questions, keys and objectives are unchanged. Two compact prototype readings remain in weeks 9 and 12; the package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Expanded the week-9 bioenergetics reading with carbon and redox bookkeeping, condition-dependent free energy, proton-motive-force coupling, uncoupling and qualified ATP-yield accounting. Existing questions, keys and objectives are unchanged. One compact prototype reading remains in week 12; the package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Expanded the week-12 pathway-regulation reading with pool balances, flux-control coefficients, isotope-tracing limits, regulatory layers and perturbation time scales. Existing questions, keys and objectives are unchanged. All four original compact prototype readings now have expanded primers; the package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Linked the first four lesson pairs to outcomes 1–4. Reassociated the preserved ligand-occupancy and pool-versus-flux questions with their matching objectives and added direct formative practice for protein structure levels and pathway regulatory layers. Existing numeric prompts and keys remain unchanged. The course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added an inactive synthetic protein-state portfolio connecting pH-dependent charge, two-state folding, denaturant stability and ligand-depletion binding under explicit assumptions. The values describe no real protein, assay or person; the course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

No graded item or answer key changed; the course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added a fifth authored outcome and linked the work into week 4. Method handbooks are cited by link only; the course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

limitations: The proposed scope focuses on proteins, enzymes and heterotrophic animal-cell metabolism. Photosynthetic energy conversion and carbon assimilation, membrane transport mechanisms and translation are not taught as dedicated strands; MIT OCW 7.05 Spring 2020 includes them, so this package is narrower than that comparator.

A proposed 14-week schedule and inactive grading-policy proposal exist but are unmeasured and unreviewed. Two synthetic-data virtual labs provide a limited paper-only sequence, not a physical laboratory sequence. Eight homework packets, midterm and final review practice and an optional protein-state project are available as open, ungraded practice; the separate homework, exam and project candidates remain inactive with private unreviewed solution/scoring drafts outside the public package. None is approved or active as graded work. Physical laboratory work is not authored.
Practice items are short formative checks; they do not demonstrate comprehensive outcome coverage or mastery, and objective associations remain provisional.
Bloom labels and structured prerequisite edges are initial authoring classifications awaiting subject-matter review.
Question answers and solution feedback are intentionally public practice authoring specifications, not restricted exam keys.

Of the 90 numeric-type practice answers in this package, 56 require a unit and 34 accept a number within a stated tolerance with the unit optional; 3 also check significant figures, and none checks dimensions. The 63 numeric fields inside data-interpretation items check the stated significant figures, and the 9 CSV-upload items check fixed summary cells only.
Total workload and weekly duration are unknown; former nominal credit values and hardcoded reading times do not establish workload.
All metabolic scenarios, cells and numbers are synthetic teaching examples; this package gives no laboratory protocols or medical advice and says nothing about any real compound, cell line or person.

Homework 1 to 8 are openly licensed formative practice with publicly inspectable answer specifications; they are not suitable as protected assignments, do not contribute to a course grade and are not the inactive homework candidates. Their datasets are synthetic, and the software checks score deterministic numeric, table-cell and choice responses only.

The week-7 midterm review and week-14 cumulative final review combine new cross-week items with earlier public items. Their answers and feedback are public practice specifications, so neither can serve as a secure exam; scores are practice feedback and do not demonstrate mastery.

The protein-state project is optional and ungraded. Its five milestones are Case studio self-checks whose private drafts are never submitted or scored; the rehearsal practice checks a separate synthetic condition C, and no software check evaluates a learner's condition A or B analysis or written interpretation. Milestone weeks are planning suggestions, not measured workload or deadlines.
intentionally_omitted: No grading policy or summative assessment is approved, and a physical laboratory sequence is not authored. Open homework, review and project practice is ungraded; the eight answer-free homework candidates, two exam candidates and the human-scored project candidate remain inactive drafts, each with a private unreviewed key or scoring draft held outside the public package. The original lessons extend a partial package.

Photosystem light harvesting and electron transport, photophosphorylation, Calvin–Benson CO₂ assimilation, membrane transport mechanisms and translation are deliberately deferred from this animal-cell-focused partial sequence; MIT OCW 7.05 Spring 2020 includes these topics.
